At Vantor Logistics, drivers who completed the new defensive-driving course had 30% fewer at-fault collisions over the following year than drivers who did not take the course. The safety director concluded that requiring all drivers to complete the course would substantially reduce the company's total at-fault collisions.

The safety director's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Drivers who completed the course had 30% fewer at-fault collisions than they themselves had in the prior year.
Drivers who voluntarily took the course were not already more cautious, on average, than those who did not take it.
At-fault collisions impose larger costs on Vantor than collisions for which its drivers are not at fault.
Most of Vantor's drivers had not taken any defensive-driving course before the new one was introduced.
The defensive-driving course is the most cost-effective safety measure available to Vantor Logistics.
explanation: This is a classic selection-effect gap. The data is observational: drivers chose to take the course. If those volunteers were already safer drivers, the 30% gap reflects who took the course, not what the course did, so mandating it for everyone need not reduce collisions. The argument therefore must assume the volunteers were not already more cautious. Negation test: if the volunteers WERE already more cautious, the course-effect could be zero and the conclusion collapses. Option B passes. (E) Cost-effectiveness is out of scope; the conclusion is only that collisions would 'substantially reduce,' not that this is the best option. (C) Relative cost of at-fault vs. not-at-fault collisions is irrelevant to whether the course works. (D) Whether drivers had taken a prior course doesn't bear on whether this course causes the reduction; negating it (many had taken one before) leaves the argument intact. (A) Restates/distorts the premise as a within-driver before/after comparison, which the study did not make; the data was a between-group comparison, so this is not what the argument relies on.

A pharmaceutical firm found that its new migraine drug eliminated headache pain within two hours in 70% of trial participants, compared with 35% for participants given a placebo. The firm argues that, because the drug outperformed the placebo by so wide a margin, the drug's chemical action on blood vessels must be responsible for the relief it provides.

The firm's argument relies on assuming which of the following?
options: The drug's effect on blood vessels is stronger than its effect on any other physiological system.
No migraine drug currently on the market relieves pain in more than 70% of patients within two hours.
The 35% of placebo participants who improved would not have improved without taking the placebo pill.
Participants who received the drug were correctly informed that they were receiving an active medication rather than a placebo.
The relief experienced by participants who took the drug was not produced merely by their expectation that an active drug would work.
explanation: The conclusion is causal and specific: the relief comes from the drug's chemical action on blood vessels. But in a trial, simply believing you've taken a real drug can produce relief (an enhanced placebo/expectation effect). The argument must assume the extra relief in the drug group wasn't just heightened expectation. Negation: if the drug group's relief WAS merely expectation-driven, the chemical-action conclusion fails. So (E) is necessary. (B) Comparison to other marketed drugs is out of scope. (C) Concerns the placebo group's improvement, not the mechanism behind the drug group's relief; negating it doesn't touch the conclusion. (A) Too strong and not required: the chemical action could relieve pain via blood vessels even if some other effect is equally strong; this is a sufficient-sounding overreach, not a necessary condition. (D) This would actually undermine a blinded trial and create the very expectation effect the argument needs to rule out; it is not an assumption the argument depends on — it is the strongest trap because at a glance it looks like it supports the drug group, but informing participants would inflate the placebo-style expectation effect rather than isolate the chemical action.

To cut energy costs, the city of Harlow replaced all 12,000 of its sodium streetlights with LED units that draw 60% less power. A council member projects that the switch will reduce the city's total streetlighting electricity bill by 60%.

The council member's projection depends on the assumption that
options: the LED units draw 60% less power than the sodium units they replaced
LED units last longer before failing than the sodium units they replaced
the LED units will not be left on for substantially more hours per night than the sodium lights they replaced
residents will not object to the different color of light the LED units produce
the price the city pays per unit of electricity will fall after the switch to LED lighting
explanation: The bill depends on power drawn AND hours of use: total energy = power × hours. The 60% bill cut follows from the 60% power cut only if usage hours stay the same. If LEDs run far more hours per night (e.g., because they're now left on longer), the bill might fall less than 60% or even rise. Negation: if LEDs ARE left on substantially longer, the 60% projection fails. So (C) is necessary. (E) A falling price per unit would make the bill drop even more, so it isn't required for a 60% cut and isn't assumed. (B) Lifespan affects replacement/maintenance cost, not the electricity bill. (D) Light color is out of scope for the electricity bill. (A) Simply restates the given premise; an argument does not 'depend on' assuming a fact it was already told.

promptHTML:
Editorial: Last year our state raised the legal age for purchasing tobacco from 18 to 21, and over the same period the smoking rate among 18-to-20-year-olds in the state fell by 15%. Critics who claim the law was ineffective are simply wrong: the decline shows the higher purchase age is working to reduce smoking in this group.

The editorial's argument requires which of the following assumptions?
options: Raising the purchase age is a more effective way to reduce youth smoking than raising tobacco taxes would be.
The new purchase age reduced smoking among 18-to-20-year-olds by a larger percentage than it reduced smoking among any older age group.
Most 18-to-20-year-olds who stopped smoking did so because they could no longer legally purchase tobacco themselves.
The smoking rate among 18-to-20-year-olds in neighboring states did not fall at all during the same period.
The 18-to-20-year-olds' smoking rate did not fall by 15% chiefly because of factors, such as a national anti-smoking campaign, that were unrelated to the state's new law.
explanation: The editorial infers causation ('the law is working') from a correlation (the law passed; smoking fell). For that inference to hold, the decline must not be primarily due to some other coincident cause. (E) states exactly this and survives the negation test: if the drop was chiefly caused by an unrelated national campaign, the editorial's causal claim is unfounded. (B) is not required — the law can be 'working' on this group regardless of how it affected older groups; this is an out-of-scope comparison. (A) is a comparison to tax policy, irrelevant to whether THIS law worked; sufficient-sounding but out of scope. (C) overspecifies the mechanism. The law could reduce smoking through social-supply reduction (fewer 21-year-old friends buying for them) without 'most' quitters being people who couldn't buy for themselves; the argument doesn't require this exact channel, so negating it doesn't sink the conclusion. (C) is the strongest trap — it sounds necessary but states a sufficient mechanism, not a necessary one. (D) Neighboring states showing no decline would strengthen the argument, but the argument doesn't logically require it; negating it (neighbors also fell) doesn't by itself prove the law did nothing, and in fact (E) already captures the alternative-cause concern more precisely.

A consumer-electronics company plans to boost annual profit by raising the price of its flagship headphones by 10%. An analyst supports the plan, noting that the headphones currently account for 40% of the company's revenue and that demand for premium audio gear has been growing steadily.

The analyst's reasoning depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Competitors will respond to the increase by raising the prices of their own premium headphones.
The company's manufacturing cost per unit of headphones will decline over the next year.
The 10% price increase will not cause a drop in unit sales large enough to offset the gain from the higher price.
Demand for premium audio gear will grow faster next year than it did this year.
The headphones will continue to account for at least 40% of the company's revenue after the price increase.
explanation: Raising price raises profit only if the higher margin per unit isn't wiped out (or worse) by fewer units sold. Profit hinges on price × quantity minus cost; a 10% price hike can reduce profit if demand is price-sensitive enough. (C) captures the necessary condition and passes the negation test: if the price hike DOES cut unit sales enough to offset the gain, the plan fails to boost profit. (A) Competitors raising prices would help, but the plan to boost profit doesn't require it; negating it doesn't break the argument. (E) Whether the product stays at 40% of revenue is a description of revenue mix, not a requirement for profit to rise; profit could rise even if the revenue share shifts. (D) The argument only needs demand not to collapse, not to grow faster than before; this is too strong. (B) A falling unit cost would add profit but isn't necessary — the price increase alone is supposed to do the work; negating it (costs flat) leaves the argument standing.

promptHTML:
Archaeologist: The 3,000-year-old settlement we excavated contained iron tools but no iron-smelting furnaces or slag, the waste left by smelting. Iron working was unknown anywhere on the continent until at least 500 years later. We therefore conclude that the settlement's iron tools were obtained through trade with peoples from across the sea.

The archaeologist's conclusion depends on assuming that
options: the peoples from across the sea valued the goods the settlement offered in exchange for iron tools
no other settlement on the continent possessed iron tools at the time the excavated settlement did
iron tools were more useful to the settlement's inhabitants than the stone tools they had used previously
the iron tools found at the settlement were manufactured fewer than 500 years before iron working became known on the continent
the settlement's iron tools were not produced by smelting carried out at the settlement itself
explanation: The conclusion is that the tools came from overseas trade. The evidence is: no furnaces/slag at the site, and no iron working on the continent for 500+ years. But the trade conclusion specifically needs to rule out local production at this very settlement. (E) states this, and the negation test confirms necessity: if the tools WERE smelted at the settlement itself, the trade conclusion is false. The absence of furnaces/slag is offered as evidence, but the conclusion still logically requires the inference that no local smelting occurred — (E) makes that link explicit. (A) Whether the overseas peoples valued the settlement's goods concerns whether trade was feasible, but the conclusion is about origin; the argument doesn't logically depend on the exchange being attractive to the other side — a tempting but unnecessary trade-logistics assumption, since the settlement could have traded for goods originating elsewhere. (C) Relative usefulness vs. stone tools is out of scope. (B) Other settlements having iron tools doesn't affect how THIS settlement got its tools; negating it changes nothing. (D) The precise manufacturing date within the 500-year window is irrelevant to the trade-vs-local-production question. (A) is the strongest trap because it sounds like a precondition for trade, but trade can occur without the other party valuing this settlement's specific goods.

Manager: Our software team's productivity, measured by features shipped per month, doubled after we moved everyone from individual offices to an open-plan workspace. To replicate this gain, we should now move our customer-support team into an open-plan workspace as well.

The manager's recommendation relies on which of the following assumptions?
options: Moving to an open plan is less expensive than other ways of improving the customer-support team's productivity.
The customer-support team is currently less productive than the software team was before its move.
An open-plan workspace would not impair the customer-support team's productivity in a way it did not impair the software team's.
The software team's productivity will continue to increase as long as it remains in the open-plan workspace.
The customer-support team's productivity can be measured by the number of features it ships per month.
explanation: The manager generalizes from one team (software) to a different team (support) with different work. The recommendation assumes the open plan won't backfire for support the way it apparently didn't for software — e.g., support work may demand quiet phone calls that an open plan disrupts. (C) survives negation: if an open plan WOULD impair support productivity (even though it didn't impair software's), moving them is a bad idea and the recommendation fails. (E) Support obviously isn't measured by 'features shipped'; the argument doesn't need this and it's nonsensical for support — a distractor that misapplies the software metric. (D) Whether the software team keeps improving is irrelevant to whether the move helps support; out of scope. (A) Relative cost is out of scope; the recommendation is that the move will 'replicate the gain,' not that it's the cheapest option. (B) The two teams' relative starting productivity isn't required; negating it (support already more productive) doesn't undermine the claim that the move would raise support's output.

promptHTML:
A regional grocery chain replaced the fluorescent lighting in 40 of its 200 stores with full-spectrum LED lighting. Over the following year, the 40 refitted stores posted average sales-per-square-foot growth of 9%, while the chain’s other stores grew only 3%. The chain’s operations director concluded that the new lighting caused shoppers to buy more, and recommended refitting all remaining stores.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the operations director’s conclusion?
options: Customer-satisfaction surveys at the refitted stores showed a marked increase in shoppers describing the stores as “pleasant.”
During the year studied, the chain ran an aggressive coupon campaign that was available to customers at all 200 stores.
Full-spectrum LED lighting consumes roughly 30% less electricity than the fluorescent lighting it replaced.
The 40 stores chosen for the lighting refit were selected at random from the chain’s 200 stores, without regard to their prior sales trends or location.
Several competing grocery chains adopted full-spectrum LED lighting during the same year and reported flat sales.
explanation:
The conclusion is causal: the new lighting caused the higher sales growth. The biggest threat to a causal claim drawn from a comparison of groups is selection bias — perhaps the 40 stores were already higher-growth stores (newer, busier locations) and would have outperformed regardless of lighting.

(D) is correct: Random selection eliminates exactly that alternative explanation. If the refitted stores were chosen with no regard to prior trends or location, then the 40 stores were, on average, representative of the chain, so the lighting is the salient difference that explains the gap. Ruling out the selection-bias alternative strengthens the causal claim.

(C) speaks to cost savings (energy), not to whether lighting drove sales — irrelevant to the causal conclusion. (A) is only mildly supportive: “pleasant” perceptions are a plausible mechanism, but customers could find many post-refit features pleasant, and pleasantness does not establish that sales rose because of lighting; it does not rule out the selection alternative. (B) is a weakener-leaning trap: a chain-wide coupon campaign applies to all stores and so cannot explain why the refitted stores grew more — and to the extent it raised baseline sales everywhere, it muddies rather than supports the lighting claim. (E) actually undercuts the conclusion: if competitors adopted the same lighting and saw flat sales, that is evidence the lighting does not drive sales.

Pharmaco is deciding whether to fund a large Phase III trial of its experimental migraine drug, X-12. In a small earlier study, patients taking X-12 reported 40% fewer migraine days than patients taking a placebo. A company analyst argued that the Phase III trial is worth funding because the earlier result shows X-12 is very likely to prove effective at preventing migraines.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the analyst’s argument?
options: In the earlier study, neither the patients nor the physicians assessing them knew which patients received X-12 and which received the placebo.
Several other drugs that reduced migraine days in small studies later failed to show any benefit in large trials.
Migraine is among the most common neurological complaints, affecting a large share of working-age adults.
X-12 can be manufactured at a cost low enough to make it profitable even at a modest selling price.
Patients in the earlier study who took X-12 reported milder side effects than patients taking the placebo.
explanation:
The conclusion is that the earlier 40%-reduction result makes X-12 likely to prove effective. The argument is only as strong as the earlier study’s reliability. A classic threat to a self-reported drug result is the placebo effect and assessor bias: patients who know they are getting the “real” drug may report fewer migraine days for psychological reasons.

(A) is correct: A double-blind design (neither patients nor assessing physicians knew the assignment) removes that confound, so the 40% gap is much more credibly attributable to the drug itself, making the earlier result a sound basis for predicting effectiveness. (D) bears on commercial viability, not on whether the drug works — irrelevant to the effectiveness conclusion. (C) addresses market size, again not effectiveness. (B) is a weakener: it gives a base-rate reason to distrust small-study results, undercutting the inference. (E) concerns side effects (tolerability), not efficacy at preventing migraines, so it does not strengthen the specific claim about effectiveness.

promptHTML:
City planners propose adding a dedicated bus lane to Harrow Road, predicting it will reduce the average commute time of all road users on that corridor. They reason that buses, freed from car traffic, will run faster, and that faster, more reliable buses will induce many current car commuters to switch to the bus, thinning the remaining car traffic.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the planners’ prediction?
options: The dedicated bus lane would be created by converting one of the corridor’s three existing car lanes, leaving two lanes for cars.
Bus fares on the Harrow Road route are lower than the cost of fuel and parking for the typical car commuter.
Surveys show that most Harrow Road car commuters say they would prefer to spend their commute time reading rather than driving.
On Harrow Road, the number of car commuters who can be persuaded to switch to the bus rises sharply once bus travel becomes even slightly faster than driving.
A similar corridor in a neighboring city added a bus lane and saw bus ridership rise by 15%.
explanation:
The conclusion is strong: average commute time for all road users falls. The chain is buses get faster → car commuters switch → car traffic thins → everyone’s commute improves. The vulnerable link, given that a car lane is being removed (A), is whether enough drivers actually switch to offset the lost road capacity for the cars that remain. If too few switch, remaining car commuters face two lanes instead of three and could be worse off, dragging down the all-users average.

(D) is correct: It guarantees the critical step — a sharp, sizable switch to the bus the moment buses become even slightly faster. A large exodus from cars is what thins car traffic enough to improve car commutes too, supporting the “all road users” claim. (A) is the trap: it supplies the mechanism’s cost (lost car capacity) and, if anything, makes the prediction harder to fulfill — it is a weakener, not a strengthener. (C) shows a preference to not drive but says nothing about whether the faster bus will actually trigger switching at scale; stated preferences routinely fail to translate into behavior, so it is only weakly supportive. (B) notes a pre-existing cost advantage of the bus that already failed to make these people switch, so it does not explain why the new lane would change behavior. (E) is tempting but insufficient: a 15% ridership rise elsewhere does not show that car traffic thinned enough to cut commute times for all users, and it may reflect new riders rather than former drivers.

A software firm noticed that the engineers it rated “top performers” in annual reviews were far more likely than other engineers to have contributed to the company’s open-source projects on weekends. The head of engineering concluded that encouraging more engineers to contribute to open-source projects on weekends would raise the overall skill level of the engineering staff.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the head of engineering’s conclusion?
options: The company’s open-source projects use the same programming languages as its commercial products.
Engineers who contributed to open-source projects on weekdays showed no review-rating advantage over non-contributors.

In a controlled program, randomly selected engineers were assigned dedicated weekend hours for open-source work; a year later their review ratings had risen more than those of engineers not in the program.
Engineers who contribute to open-source projects report higher job satisfaction than those who do not.
Top-performing engineers tend to be more intrinsically curious and self-motivated than their peers.
explanation:
The conclusion treats a correlation (top performers contribute more on weekends) as causal and forward-looking: getting more engineers to contribute will raise skill. The chief alternative is reverse causation / common cause — maybe skilled, motivated engineers both perform well and choose to contribute, so pushing average engineers to contribute would not make them better.

(C) is correct: A randomized intervention in which assigning weekend open-source hours caused ratings to rise directly establishes the causal direction the conclusion needs, ruling out the “skilled people self-select into contributing” story. (D) concerns satisfaction, not skill, and could reflect the same self-selection — irrelevant to the skill conclusion. (A) offers a plausible mechanism (shared languages) but does not show contributing raises skill rather than the reverse, so it is only mildly supportive. (E) is a weakener: it names a common cause (curiosity/self-motivation) that could produce both the high ratings and the contributing, undercutting the causal claim. (B) is a subtle trap: it might seem to isolate “weekend” as special, but it equally fits the self-selection story (the most driven engineers give up their weekends) and does nothing to show that inducing contribution raises skill.

An airline introduced a “quick-turn” procedure at its hub, cutting the time aircraft spend at the gate between flights. In the six months after the change, the airline’s rate of delayed departures from the hub fell by 20%. An executive concluded that the quick-turn procedure was responsible for the improvement in on-time departures.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the executive’s conclusion?
options: At a comparable hub of the same airline where the quick-turn procedure was not introduced, the rate of delayed departures was unchanged over the same six months.
The quick-turn procedure required the airline to hire additional ground crew at the hub.
The six months following the change happened to include unusually mild weather at the hub.
Most departure delays at the hub had historically been caused by late arrival of the inbound aircraft, not by gate time.
After the quick-turn procedure was introduced, the airline’s passenger satisfaction scores at the hub improved.
explanation:
The conclusion attributes the 20% drop in delays to the quick-turn procedure. The main rivals are (i) some other factor changed at the hub during the same period (e.g., weather, schedule changes) and (ii) the procedure does not actually address the real cause of delays.

(A) is correct: A control hub of the same airline, same six months, no quick-turn, no improvement, isolates the procedure as the operative difference. It rules out airline-wide or seasonal factors that would have affected both hubs, sharply strengthening the causal claim. (E) reports satisfaction, not on-time performance, and could stem from many things — irrelevant. (C) is a weakener: mild weather is a competing explanation for fewer delays, so it undermines attributing the improvement to the procedure. (D) is the strongest trap — it is a weakener disguised as detail: if most delays came from late inbound aircraft rather than gate time, then cutting gate time should not have driven the improvement, casting doubt on the conclusion. (B) describes an input cost of the procedure but says nothing about whether the procedure, rather than something else, caused the delay reduction.

Archaeologists found that a 3,000-year-old coastal settlement was abandoned abruptly. At the abandonment layer they recovered large quantities of fish bones but almost no remains of the shellfish that dominate every earlier layer. They hypothesize that a sudden collapse of the local shellfish population forced the inhabitants to leave when fishing alone could not feed them.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the archaeologists’ hypothesis?
options: Settlements elsewhere on the same coast continued to harvest shellfish for centuries after this site was abandoned.
Sediment cores from the settlement’s shoreline show that, at the time of abandonment, a change in water chemistry made the bay uninhabitable for the local shellfish species.
The fish species represented in the abandonment layer are ones that can be caught year-round in the bay.
Earlier layers at the site contain occasional arrowheads, suggesting the inhabitants also hunted game.
Pottery styles found in the abandonment layer match those of a settlement 200 kilometers inland.
explanation:
The hypothesis has two parts: a shellfish-population collapse occurred, and it drove abandonment because fishing alone was insufficient. The absence of shellfish remains is the key clue, but it has an innocent alternative: maybe the inhabitants simply stopped collecting shellfish (a dietary shift), not that the shellfish died off.

(B) is correct: Independent physical evidence (water chemistry made the bay uninhabitable for the shellfish) directly confirms an actual population collapse, the linchpin of the hypothesis, and rules out the “they just chose to stop eating shellfish” alternative. (E) tells us where people may have gone, not why they left, and is consistent with many causes of departure — not strengthening the shellfish-collapse mechanism. (C) is a subtle weakener: if fish were available year-round, that undercuts the claim that the loss of shellfish made the site unlivable. (D) suggests an additional food source (game), which would weaken the claim that losing shellfish forced abandonment. (A) is the strongest distractor and a weakener: if nearby coastal sites kept harvesting shellfish for centuries, that argues against a region-wide shellfish collapse, undermining the hypothesis for this site.

A national retailer is testing whether to install in-store coffee bars. In a pilot, it added coffee bars to 25 stores; over the next quarter, those stores’ total revenue rose 12% versus the prior quarter, while comparable stores without coffee bars rose 4%. The retailer’s CFO argues that the coffee bars raised revenue by drawing in additional shoppers who then bought other merchandise, and recommends a nationwide rollout.

Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the CFO’s argument?
options: The 25 pilot stores were located in densely populated urban areas with heavy foot traffic.
Customers who bought coffee at the pilot stores spent, on average, about the same per visit on other merchandise as they had before the coffee bars opened.
In the pilot stores, sales of non-coffee merchandise — not just coffee itself — rose substantially more than in the comparable stores, and store traffic counts increased.
Several of the retailer’s competitors have recently added coffee bars to their own stores.
Across the 25 pilot stores, the coffee bars themselves operated at a healthy profit margin during the quarter.
explanation:
The CFO’s specific mechanism is that coffee bars drew in additional shoppers who then bought other merchandise. So the conclusion needs more than “revenue rose” — it needs evidence that (i) traffic increased and (ii) the lift came from other merchandise, not merely coffee sales counted as revenue.

(C) is correct: Higher non-coffee merchandise sales plus increased traffic counts match the stated mechanism precisely — more shoppers came in and bought other goods — ruling out the deflating alternative that the entire revenue bump was just coffee revenue. (E) is a trap: a profitable coffee bar shows coffee itself sells, but that is consistent with the lift being only coffee revenue, which does not support the “buy other merchandise” claim. (B) is a weakener: if coffee buyers spent the same on other merchandise as before, the bars did not boost other-merchandise spending per shopper, undercutting the mechanism. (A) raises a selection concern (urban, high-traffic pilot stores may not generalize) and, if anything, weakens the case for a nationwide rollout. (D) reports competitor behavior, which neither confirms the traffic-plus-merchandise mechanism nor that rollout will pay off.

A regional grocery chain installed self-checkout kiosks in all 40 of its stores last year. In the six months after installation, the average transaction time at those stores fell by 22%, and customer-satisfaction survey scores rose. The chain's operations director concludes that converting the remaining checkout lanes to self-checkout will further reduce transaction times and raise satisfaction scores.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the operations director's conclusion?
options: Customers who use self-checkout kiosks tend to buy fewer items per visit than customers who use staffed lanes.
The self-checkout kiosks cost roughly three times as much to install and maintain as a conventional staffed lane handling the same volume of customers.
The satisfaction-survey scores were collected by store staff at the exit, and response rates were higher at stores with shorter checkout lines.

The reduction in average transaction time was concentrated almost entirely among customers buying fewer than ten items, who self-selected into the kiosks; customers with full carts still strongly prefer staffed lanes and find self-checkout slower for large orders.
A competing grocery chain that converted entirely to self-checkout three years ago has since seen its market share grow.
explanation:
The conclusion is that converting the remaining lanes to self-checkout will further cut times and raise satisfaction. The argument's hidden assumption is that the benefits seen so far generalize to the customers who currently use staffed lanes.

Correct (D): It shows the observed gains came almost entirely from small-basket customers who chose the kiosks, while full-cart customers find self-checkout slower and prefer staffed lanes. Forcing those remaining customers onto self-checkout would therefore not extend the gains — and could reverse them. This directly attacks the load-bearing assumption that the benefit transfers to the remaining lanes' users.

Why the traps fail: (B) Cost is irrelevant — the conclusion is about transaction times and satisfaction, not budget. (A) Fewer items per visit doesn't bear on transaction time or satisfaction, and could even be a reason times fell. (E) A competitor's market-share growth is a weak, confounded analogy and doesn't address whether this chain's remaining customers benefit; it arguably mildly strengthens. (C) This questions the satisfaction data's reliability, but only one of the two effects, and it is speculative about direction; (D) undercuts both effects directly via the actual mechanism. The most precise, scope-matched weakener is (D).

Pharmaceutical researchers tested a new compound, Zelaxin, intended to lower blood pressure. In a six-month trial, patients taking Zelaxin showed an average drop in systolic blood pressure of 14 points, while patients taking a placebo showed an average drop of only 3 points. The researchers concluded that Zelaxin is an effective blood-pressure-lowering agent and recommended it for approval.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researchers' conclusion?
options: A small number of patients in the Zelaxin group withdrew before the trial ended because of mild dizziness.
The 3-point drop in the placebo group is consistent with drops seen in other placebo arms of blood-pressure trials.
At a dose twice that used in the trial, Zelaxin lowered systolic blood pressure by 19 points in an earlier pilot study.

Patients in the Zelaxin group were, on average, eight years younger than patients in the placebo group, and blood pressure in this trial declined faster with the dietary counseling that all participants received the younger they were.
Zelaxin is chemically similar to an older drug that was withdrawn from the market for reasons unrelated to its blood-pressure effects.
explanation:
The conclusion infers Zelaxin's efficacy from the difference between the two groups' average drops. That inference assumes the two groups were comparable except for the drug — i.e., that the larger drop is attributable to Zelaxin rather than to some confounding difference between the groups.

Correct (D): It identifies exactly such a confounder. If the Zelaxin group was substantially younger, and younger patients dropped more from the shared dietary counseling, then the group's larger decline may be due to age, not the drug. This breaks the causal link the conclusion depends on. The randomization apparently failed to balance age, so the between-group comparison is invalid.

Why the traps fail: (A) A few withdrawals for mild dizziness is a minor safety note, not a challenge to efficacy. (B) Saying the placebo drop is typical actually supports treating the difference as real — it mildly strengthens. (E) Chemical similarity to a drug withdrawn for unrelated reasons says nothing about Zelaxin's blood-pressure effect. (C) A bigger drop at a higher dose strengthens the case that Zelaxin lowers blood pressure. Only (D) supplies an alternative explanation for the observed group difference.

City planners noted that the downtown district with the highest density of bicycle lanes also has the highest rate of cycling commuters. They concluded that building more bicycle lanes in the city's outer neighborhoods would substantially increase the number of residents who commute by bicycle in those neighborhoods.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the planners' conclusion?
options: The downtown district's bicycle lanes were originally built in response to an unusually high pre-existing population of cycling commuters who had lobbied for them.
Cycling commuters in the downtown district report higher job satisfaction than commuters who drive.
Outer neighborhoods have wider roads than the downtown district, making bicycle-lane construction less expensive there.
The downtown district has more retail businesses per square mile than the outer neighborhoods do.
Some residents of the outer neighborhoods already commute downtown by bicycle using the downtown lanes.
explanation:
The argument treats the correlation between lane density and cycling rates as evidence that lanes cause cycling, then projects that causation onto the outer neighborhoods. The hidden assumption is that the lanes drove the cycling, rather than the reverse.

Correct (A): If the lanes were built because there was already a large cycling population, then high cycling caused the lanes, not the other way around. That reverses the causal arrow the conclusion relies on, so there is no basis to expect lanes to generate cyclists where the prior demand doesn't already exist.

Why the traps fail: (B) Job satisfaction is irrelevant to whether lanes increase cycling numbers. (C) Cheaper construction in outer neighborhoods is about cost/feasibility, not about whether lanes will raise cycling rates. (E) That some outer residents already cycle downtown is neutral — it doesn't tell us new lanes would convert non-cyclists. (D) Retail density is a possible alternative driver of downtown cycling, but it's vague and doesn't directly reverse or sever the lane-to-cycling link the way (A) does. (A) is the cleanest reversal of causation.

A software company switched its 200-person engineering division to a four-day workweek. Over the following quarter, the number of software features shipped per week rose by 15% compared with the previous quarter. The CEO argues that the compressed schedule made engineers more productive and plans to extend the four-day week to the company's 150-person customer-support division to boost its output similarly.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the CEO's plan to extend the four-day week to customer support?
options: Customer-support employees have expressed strong interest in a four-day workweek.

Customer-support work consists of responding to a continuous, externally driven inflow of tickets that must be handled the day they arrive, whereas engineering work is self-paced project work that can be batched and front-loaded.
Some features shipped during the quarter were smaller than the features shipped in the previous quarter.
The engineering division's 15% increase in features shipped was measured against a quarter that included a two-week company-wide holiday shutdown.
During the quarter the engineering division adopted the four-day week, it also completed a long-planned migration to faster build-and-deployment tooling.
explanation:
The plan assumes that what boosted engineering output will transfer to customer support. Note the question asks specifically what weakens extending the schedule to support — so a confounder in the engineering result, while it weakens the productivity claim, is less on-point than something showing the two kinds of work differ in a way that defeats the transfer.

Correct (B): It shows a structural difference: support handles a continuous, day-of inflow of tickets that can't be batched, whereas engineering work is self-paced and can be front-loaded into four days. Compressing support into four days would leave a day with no coverage for time-sensitive tickets, so the mechanism that may have helped engineering can't operate the same way in support. This directly attacks the transferability the plan depends on.

Why the traps fail: (E) and (D) are confounders that undermine whether the four-day week truly raised engineering output — tempting, but they attack the premise about engineering, not the specific extension to support, and the question targets the extension. (A) Employee interest is about morale/buy-in, not output, and if anything supports the plan. (C) Smaller features would undercut the 15% figure but, again, concerns engineering's result, not the support transfer. (B) is the only option keyed to why support specifically would not benefit.

An airline introduced a $25 fee for checked bags. In the year after the fee took effect, the airline's on-time departure rate improved noticeably. An analyst attributes the improvement to the fee: with fewer checked bags to load, ground crews could turn planes around faster, reducing departure delays.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's explanation?
options: The $25 fee generated substantial additional revenue for the airline.
Passengers who paid the checked-bag fee reported lower overall satisfaction with the airline.
Competing airlines that did not introduce checked-bag fees saw no change in their on-time departure rates over the same year.
After the fee was introduced, many passengers carried more bags into the cabin, and the resulting boarding congestion lengthened the time needed to seat passengers and close the aircraft doors.
The airline reduced the number of checked bags per flight by about 30% after introducing the fee.
explanation:
The analyst claims the bag fee improved on-time departures via faster ground turnaround. The reasoning assumes the net effect of fewer checked bags is faster departures — ignoring offsetting effects elsewhere in the departure process.

Correct (D): It identifies a countervailing consequence of the fee: passengers shifted bags into the cabin, causing boarding congestion that lengthens the seating-and-door-close step, which also gates on-time departure. This undercuts the claim that the fee, through reduced checked bags, was the cause of the improvement — the fee introduced a delay-increasing effect, so the on-time gain is more likely due to something else. It weakens the causal explanation.

Why the traps fail: (A) Revenue is irrelevant to departure timing. (C) Competitors seeing no change while this airline improved actually strengthens the idea that the airline's own change (the fee) caused its improvement. (E) Confirming a 30% drop in checked bags supports the analyst's mechanism. (B) Lower satisfaction doesn't bear on whether the fee caused the on-time improvement. Only (D) provides a reason the fee would not, on net, speed departures.

promptHTML:
To reduce employee turnover, a call center raised starting wages by 20%. In the year following the raise, annual turnover fell from 45% to 30%. Management concluded that the wage increase was responsible for the drop and that a further wage increase would reduce turnover even more.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens management's reasoning that a further wage increase would reduce turnover even more?
options: The 20% raise brought the call center's starting wage from well below the local market average up to roughly the market average, and exit interviews indicate that almost all remaining departures are now driven by employees seeking different kinds of work rather than higher pay.
Employees who received the raise reported higher job satisfaction in an internal survey.
During the year after the raise, the regional unemployment rate rose, giving workers fewer alternative job opportunities.
The call center's main competitor for labor also raised its starting wages by 20% during the same year.
The 20% raise increased the call center's total labor costs by a significant amount.
explanation:
Management's forecast — that more wage increase yields more turnover reduction — assumes the relationship between pay and turnover is roughly linear and that pay is still the binding constraint on departures. The weakener should attack that extrapolation.

Correct (A): It shows the first raise closed a below-market gap, and that remaining departures are now driven by people wanting different work, not more money. If pay is no longer the reason people leave, then pushing wages above market would address a cause that has largely been eliminated, so further raises would not produce a comparable further drop. This breaks the assumed continued pay-turnover link specifically for the next increase.

Why the traps fail: (C) Rising unemployment is a confounder for the past drop (it could explain part of the 45%→30% fall), which weakens the causal claim about the first raise — but the question targets the forecast about a further raise, and (A) is keyed to that. (D) A competitor matching the raise might erode the first raise's edge, but it's about the past effect and is indirect. (B) Higher satisfaction supports, not weakens. (E) Cost is irrelevant to whether turnover would fall further. (A) most directly defeats the extrapolation.

A national park introduced a permit system that caps the number of daily hikers on its most popular trail. Park officials report that since the cap took effect, the trail's vegetation along the path has visibly recovered. They conclude that the permit cap caused the recovery and that imposing identical caps on the park's other heavily used trails will restore vegetation on those trails too.

Which of the following, if true, most weakens the officials' conclusion?
options: The permit system generated complaints from hikers who were turned away on busy weekends.
The other heavily used trails attract roughly the same number of hikers per day as the capped trail did before its cap.
Vegetation on the capped trail recovered faster than officials had initially predicted.
On the capped trail, the vegetation recovery occurred only after the park also rerouted the path away from a fragile slope and laid down a gravel surface that keeps hikers off the surrounding soil.
The park's total annual visitor count has remained steady since the permit system was introduced.
explanation:
Officials credit the cap for the recovery and generalize: identical caps elsewhere will produce the same recovery. The assumption is that the cap, by itself, was the cause — so the result will replicate wherever a cap is imposed.

Correct (D): It reveals that the recovery on the capped trail coincided with two other interventions — rerouting the path off a fragile slope and laying gravel to keep hikers off the soil. If those changes, not the cap, drove the recovery, then imposing only a cap on other trails (without the rerouting and surfacing) would not reproduce the result. This severs the cap-to-recovery causal link the generalization depends on.

Why the traps fail: (A) Hiker complaints are irrelevant to whether vegetation recovers. (B) Similar hiker numbers on other trails make them comparable, which mildly supports applying the same approach. (C) Faster-than-predicted recovery doesn't tell us the cap caused it. (E) Steady total visitor count is neutral and arguably consistent with the cap merely redistributing hikers. Only (D) supplies an alternative cause that wouldn't carry over to the other trails.

At Meridian Logistics, every driver who completed the new defensive-driving course was reassigned to long-haul routes. No driver on a short-haul route has been involved in an at-fault collision this year. Furthermore, every driver who has been involved in an at-fault collision this year completed the defensive-driving course.

If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Drivers who did not complete the course are less likely to have an at-fault collision than those who did.
All long-haul drivers completed the defensive-driving course.
Every driver involved in an at-fault collision this year is currently on a long-haul route.
No driver on a long-haul route has been involved in an at-fault collision this year.
Every driver who completed the defensive-driving course has been involved in an at-fault collision this year.
explanation:
Trace the chain. Every at-fault driver completed the course (premise 3). Every course-completer was reassigned to long-haul (premise 1). Therefore every at-fault driver is on a long-haul route. That is exactly choice C, and it must be true.

Why the others fail:
E reverses the direction: completing the course does not force an at-fault collision; the premise only runs collision ⇒ course, not course ⇒ collision. Could-be-false.
D is contradicted by the chain we just built — at-fault drivers exist on long-haul routes (in fact ALL of them are there), so it is false, not merely unsupported. The premise that short-haul drivers have had no collisions tells us nothing forcing long-haul to be collision-free; the deduction actually points the other way.
A introduces a comparative likelihood claim. The stimulus is purely categorical (all/none); it gives no base rates or probabilities, so a 'less likely' claim is unsupported.
B reverses premise 1: course-completers became long-haul drivers, but that does not establish that every long-haul driver took the course (some may have been on long-haul already). Could-be-false.

A regional bank found that among customers who opened a high-yield savings account last year, those who also used the bank's budgeting app maintained, on average, balances 30% higher than those who did not use the app. The bank drew no causal conclusion, but its analysts noted that app users and non-users were similar in income and account tenure.

Which of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
options: The budgeting app is the only factor that distinguishes high-balance customers from low-balance customers.
Using the budgeting app causes customers to maintain higher savings balances.
If a non-user adopts the app, that customer's balance will rise by 30%.
Customers who do not use the budgeting app have below-average incomes.
Among these customers, average balance differed between app users and non-users even though the two groups were comparable in income and tenure.
explanation:
The stimulus reports a 30% average-balance gap between app users and non-users, and separately reports that the two groups were similar in income and tenure. Choice E simply restates these two facts joined together — a balance difference existed despite comparability on income and tenure. That is directly supported.

Why the others fail:
B and C assert causation/prediction; the passage explicitly draws no causal conclusion, and similarity on two variables does not rule out other confounders, so a causal or predictive claim is too strong.
D contradicts the stated similarity in income — if the groups were similar in income, non-users are not characterized as below-average earners.
A ('the only factor') is far too strong; controlling for income and tenure does not establish that no other variable matters. The phrase 'only factor' is a classic over-reach trap on inference questions.

promptHTML:
Every supplier that passed the factory's Tier-1 safety audit also received a renewed contract. Some suppliers that received a renewed contract did not pass the Tier-1 audit. No supplier located outside the country passed the Tier-1 audit. At least one supplier passed the Tier-1 audit.

Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the statements above?
options: Every supplier located outside the country failed to receive a renewed contract.
No supplier that failed the Tier-1 audit received a renewed contract.
Every supplier that received a renewed contract passed the Tier-1 audit.
Some suppliers that received a renewed contract are located outside the country.
At least one domestic supplier received a renewed contract.
explanation:
Use the four premises. Premise 4 guarantees at least one supplier passed Tier-1. By premise 3, every Tier-1 passer is located in-country (domestic), since no outside-country supplier passed. By premise 1, every Tier-1 passer received a renewed contract. Therefore that passing supplier is a domestic supplier that received a renewed contract — choice E must be true.

Why the others fail:
D Could-be-false: it is consistent with the premises that all renewed-contract suppliers are domestic; nothing forces any foreign supplier into the renewed group.
A Too strong / not forced: a foreign supplier fails Tier-1 (premise 3), but premise 1 only links PASSING to renewal, not failing to non-renewal. Premise 2 shows non-passers CAN still be renewed, so a foreign supplier could have a renewed contract. Not guaranteed false-for-all-foreign.
B Directly contradicted by premise 2, which states some renewed suppliers did NOT pass the audit.
C Reverses premise 1 and is contradicted by premise 2 (renewed suppliers who did not pass exist).
The premise added in the stimulus (at least one passer) is what makes E airtight rather than vacuous — the intended trap is to dismiss E as resting on a possibly-empty passer set.

In a municipal survey, every resident either commutes by car or does not, and supporters and opponents of a new transit levy were each counted. Among residents who commute by car, supporters of the levy were a majority. Across all residents, opponents of the levy outnumbered supporters.

Which of the following must be true?
options: Every resident who opposes the levy commutes by car.
Among residents who do not commute by car, opponents of the levy outnumber supporters.
A majority of residents commute by car.
Most car commuters oppose the levy.
Most levy supporters commute by car.
explanation:
Partition residents into car commuters and non-car commuters. Let (car S, car O) and (non-car S, non-car O) be the supporter/opponent counts in each group. Premise: car S > car O. Overall: total O > total S, i.e., (car O + non-car O) > (car S + non-car S). Rearranging, (non-car O) − (non-car S) > (car S) − (car O) > 0. So non-car O > non-car S — among non-car commuters, opponents outnumber supporters. Choice B must be true.

Why the others fail:
C Nothing fixes the size of the car-commuter group relative to the whole population; car commuters could be a small minority while still having an internal supporter majority. Could-be-false.
E reverses the relationship: a supporter majority WITHIN car commuters does not imply that most supporters are car commuters (depends on how many supporters live in the non-car group). Could-be-false.
D directly contradicts the premise that supporters were a majority among car commuters.
A is far too strong and is contradicted by the derivation, which shows opponents exist among non-car commuters.

promptHTML:
An online retailer reports that whenever it offers free two-day shipping, its cart-abandonment rate falls below 20%. Last quarter, the abandonment rate never fell below 20% in any week. The retailer offers free two-day shipping only during promotional weeks.

Which of the following can be properly concluded from the statements above?
options: Last quarter's abandonment rate was always exactly 20%.
Every promotional week last quarter had an abandonment rate below 20%.
No week last quarter was a promotional week.
Free two-day shipping is the only way to push abandonment below 20%.
The retailer offered free two-day shipping in no week last quarter.
explanation:
Premise: offering free two-day shipping ⇒ abandonment below 20%. Last quarter, abandonment was NEVER below 20%. By contraposition (modus tollens), free two-day shipping was offered in no week last quarter — exactly choice E.

Why the others fail:
C overreaches. We learned shipping was not offered, but the retailer offers free shipping ONLY during promotional weeks — that means free shipping implies a promotional week, not that every promotional week has free shipping. Promotional weeks could exist without the offer, so we cannot conclude there were none. Could-be-false.
B is contradicted: if any promotional week occurred, its abandonment rate was at or above 20% (the rate was never below 20% all quarter), so 'below 20%' is false for it.
D 'the only way' is too strong; the premise gives a sufficient condition (shipping ⇒ low abandonment), not a necessary one. Other causes of low abandonment are not excluded.
A 'exactly 20%' is unsupported; 'never below 20%' permits rates above 20%, not only equal to 20%. Could-be-false.

promptHTML:
A venture fund's analysis of its portfolio showed that startups that raised a Series B within 18 months of their Series A had a higher five-year survival rate than those that did not. It also found that startups led by founders with prior exits raised a Series B within 18 months at a higher rate than startups led by first-time founders, and that rate was greater than zero. Every founder with a prior exit in the portfolio led a startup in enterprise software.

Which of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?
options: Founders with prior exits cause their startups to survive longer.
Some enterprise-software startups in the portfolio raised a Series B within 18 months of their Series A.
First-time founders in the portfolio had lower five-year survival rates than founders with prior exits.
Most startups in the portfolio that survived five years raised a Series B within 18 months.
Every enterprise-software startup in the portfolio was led by a founder with a prior exit.
explanation:
Chain the categorical claims. Prior-exit founders raised a Series B within 18 months at a rate greater than zero, so at least one prior-exit-led startup did raise a Series B within 18 months. Every prior-exit founder led an enterprise-software startup. Therefore at least one enterprise-software startup raised a Series B within 18 months — choice B is supported.

Why the others fail:
A asserts causation ('cause ... survive longer'); the data are observational correlations (survival linked to fast Series B; prior exits linked to fast Series B), which cannot establish that prior exits CAUSE survival. Too strong.
C chains two correlations into a survival comparison between founder types, but the survival statistic was tied to Series-B timing, not directly to founder experience; first-time founders who happened to raise a fast Series B could survive at the higher rate. Not forced.
D reverses the conditional: a higher survival rate AMONG fast-Series-B startups does not imply that most SURVIVORS were fast-Series-B startups (that depends on group sizes and the survival rate of the other group). Could-be-false.
E reverses premise 3: all prior-exit founders led enterprise-software startups, but enterprise-software startups could also be led by first-time founders. Could-be-false.

Last year, Veraline Foods replaced the artificial preservative in its flagship soup with a natural one and prominently advertised the change. Over the following six months, unit sales of that soup rose 14%. Veraline's marketing director concludes that the switch to the natural preservative was responsible for the sales increase.

Which of the following would be most useful to investigate in order to evaluate the marketing director's conclusion?
options: Whether sales of Veraline's other soups, which were not reformulated or advertised, rose by a similar percentage over the same six months
Whether the natural preservative costs more per unit than the artificial one it replaced
Whether consumers can taste any difference between soup made with the natural preservative and soup made with the artificial one
Whether the natural preservative keeps the soup fresh for as long as the artificial preservative did
Whether Veraline's competitors also use natural preservatives in their comparable soups
explanation:
The conclusion is that the preservative switch caused the 14% rise. To evaluate a causal claim like this, the most useful move is to check for an alternative explanation that would have raised sales anyway. Option (A) does exactly that: if Veraline's other, unchanged-and-unadvertised soups also rose ~14% over the same period, some general factor (a market-wide demand bump, a pricing or distribution change, seasonality) is the more likely cause, and the conclusion is weakened; if those other soups were flat, the conclusion is strengthened. The answer to (A) swings the conclusion, which is the hallmark of the right evaluate answer.

(E) is irrelevant: what competitors do does not tell us why Veraline's own sales moved. (B) Cost per unit bears on profitability, not on whether the switch drove the sales increase — sales could rise regardless of cost. (C) Whether consumers can taste a difference does not address the cause of the sales change; the ad campaign touted the change as 'natural,' not as better-tasting, so a taste difference is beside the point. (D) Shelf life affects spoilage and returns, not the stated 14% sales rise. Only (A)'s answer can change the conclusion either way.

To cut overtime costs, the city transit authority installed automated fare gates at its 40 busiest stations; the remaining 60 stations kept human fare collectors. In the year after installation, the 40 automated stations together recorded 22% fewer fare-evasion incidents than they had the year before. The authority's analyst concludes that automated gates reduce fare evasion more effectively than human collectors do.

The answer to which of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the analyst's conclusion?
options: Are the 40 automated stations located in neighborhoods with higher average incomes than the 60 staffed stations?
Did the number of human collectors employed by the authority decline after the automated gates were installed?
Do automated gates allow passengers to board more quickly during peak hours than human collectors do?
Did the cost of installing and maintaining the automated gates exceed the overtime savings the authority achieved?
Over the same year, did recorded fare-evasion incidents at the 60 stations that kept human collectors rise, fall, or stay the same?
explanation:
The conclusion is a comparative causal claim: automated gates reduce evasion more effectively than human collectors. The before-after drop at automated stations alone cannot establish that, because evasion might have fallen everywhere for some independent reason (more enforcement campaigns, a fare cut, better signage, a downturn in ridership of the evading demographic). Option (E) supplies the missing comparison group. If evasion at the human-staffed stations also fell ~22%, the automation gets no special credit and the conclusion collapses; if it stayed flat or rose while automated stations dropped, the conclusion is supported. The answer swings the conclusion, so (E) is the test that evaluates it.

(A) is the tempting trap: income could correlate with evasion. But it does not address the conclusion as stated, because we are told the automated stations' evasion fell year over year — a stable neighborhood-income difference was already present in the baseline year and cannot explain a year-over-year change. (D) and (B) concern cost and staffing, not the effectiveness comparison. (C) Boarding speed is a different benefit entirely and says nothing about evasion. Only (E)'s answer can move the conclusion either way.

A pharmaceutical startup reports that in its trial, patients who took its new drug for migraines reported, on average, 30% fewer migraine days per month than they had before the trial. The company argues that the drug is an effective treatment for chronic migraines and should be approved.

Which of the following would it be most useful to determine in order to evaluate the company's argument?
options: Whether the patients in the trial had been correctly diagnosed with chronic migraines before enrolling
Whether the drug is more expensive to manufacture than competing migraine medications
Whether the 30% reduction was sustained for the full duration of the trial or concentrated in its first week
Whether patients given an inactive placebo in the same trial also reported a substantial drop in migraine days
Whether the drug produces side effects more severe than those of migraine treatments already on the market
explanation:
The argument infers drug efficacy from a 30% before-versus-after drop in migraine days. The central vulnerability is that self-reported symptom counts often fall in trials regardless of the active ingredient — the placebo effect, regression to the mean, and reporting bias all push the same way. Option (D) tests precisely this: if placebo patients showed a similar drop, the 30% cannot be credited to the drug and the argument fails; if placebo patients did not improve, the drug's effect stands out and the argument is strengthened. That swing is what an evaluate answer must produce.

(E) Side-effect severity bears on the risk-benefit and on whether it should be preferred, but not on whether the drug works; even a drug with bad side effects can be efficacious. (C) is tempting, but a drop concentrated early versus spread evenly would still be a real reduction relative to baseline; without a control it tells us nothing about cause. (A) Confirming the diagnosis matters for generalizability but does not bear on whether the observed change was caused by the drug. (B) Manufacturing cost is irrelevant to efficacy. Only (D) can change the conclusion either way.

promptHTML:
Editorial: Our state should adopt mandatory composting, as the neighboring state of Aldoria did three years ago. Since Aldoria's mandate took effect, the total tonnage of waste its residents send to landfills has dropped by 35%. Clearly, a composting mandate is the way to achieve a large reduction in landfill waste.

The answer to which of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the editorial's reasoning?
options: Has the cost of waste disposal for the average Aldorian household risen or fallen since the composting mandate took effect?
Do a majority of our state's residents say they would support a mandatory composting program?
Does our state currently send more total tonnage to landfills each year than Aldoria did before its mandate?
In the same three-year period, did Aldoria also enact a separate ban on single-use plastics or a major recycling expansion that would independently reduce landfill tonnage?
Is the climate in our state similar enough to Aldoria's that food waste would decompose at comparable rates in compost facilities?
explanation:
The editorial credits Aldoria's composting mandate with the 35% landfill drop, then recommends copying it. The reasoning is vulnerable if some other policy enacted in the same window did the heavy lifting. Option (D) targets exactly that confound: if Aldoria simultaneously banned single-use plastics or expanded recycling, those measures could account for much of the 35%, and attributing the drop to composting — and recommending composting alone — is unwarranted; if no such measures existed, the composting attribution is much stronger. The answer swings the conclusion, which is what an evaluate question requires.

(C) Whether our state landfills more tonnage than Aldoria did is about scale, not about whether composting caused the drop. (B) Resident support bears on political feasibility, not on whether the mandate works. (E) Climate-driven decomposition rates are a tempting 'will it transfer?' concern, but the editorial's inference rests on whether composting caused Aldoria's drop, and decomposition speed does not address that causal link or the alternative-cause problem. (A) Household cost is a side issue. Only (D) can change the conclusion either way.

promptHTML:
A logistics firm switched its delivery fleet from gasoline vans to electric vans, projecting that it would cut its annual fuel-and-energy spending by at least 40%. After the switch, the firm found that its combined annual spending on vehicle energy had indeed fallen by 42% compared with the previous year. Management concludes that the switch to electric vans achieved the projected savings.

Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating management's conclusion?
options: Whether the firm's drivers found the electric vans easier to operate than the gasoline vans
Whether the electric vans require less frequent routine maintenance than the gasoline vans did
Whether the average market price of gasoline during the year after the switch was roughly the same as it had been the year before
Whether the price of electricity is expected to rise over the next several years
Whether competing logistics firms have also begun adopting electric delivery vans
explanation:
Management attributes the entire 42% drop in energy spending to the switch to electric. But spending is price times quantity, and a confound lurks in price. Option (C) isolates it: if gasoline prices had crashed in the year after the switch, then even the firm's old gasoline fleet would have cost much less to run, so part of the 42% reflects cheaper fuel rather than the technology change — weakening the conclusion. Conversely, if gas prices were roughly flat, the saving is attributable to the switch, strengthening it. Because the answer can move the conclusion either way, (C) is the right evaluate choice. (A tempting subtlety: one might think a comparison of old gas prices versus new electricity prices matters, but the conclusion is about whether the switch produced the realized saving relative to staying on gas, so the relevant counterfactual is what running the gas fleet would have cost in the new year — i.e., gasoline prices in that year.)

(D) Future electricity prices do not bear on a saving already realized this past year. (B) Maintenance frequency is a separate cost category, not the fuel-and-energy spending the projection covered. (E) Competitor adoption is irrelevant to this firm's realized savings. (A) Driver ease of operation says nothing about cost. Only (C) can change the conclusion.
