A university found that students who participated in its new peer-tutoring program earned higher final grades, on average, than students who did not participate. The dean concludes that the peer-tutoring program improves students' academic performance and plans to make it mandatory for all students.

The answer to which of the following questions would be most useful in evaluating the dean's conclusion?
options: Do students at other universities with similar peer-tutoring programs report being satisfied with them?
Does the university have enough trained peer tutors to serve every student if the program is made mandatory?
Are the final grades in the courses covered by the program assigned on a curve relative to all students in the course?
Were the students who chose to participate in the peer-tutoring program already earning higher grades than non-participants before the program began?
Did participating students spend more total hours studying than non-participating students during the term?
explanation:
The program was voluntary, so the comparison is between self-selected participants and everyone else — a textbook selection-bias setup. The dean's causal conclusion ('the program improves performance') is only warranted if the two groups were comparable to start. Option (D) tests this directly: if participants were already stronger students before the program, their higher final grades may reflect pre-existing ability rather than any effect of tutoring, gutting the conclusion; if the groups started equal, the grade gap is better attributed to the program, supporting it. The answer swings the conclusion, so (D) is the evaluate answer.

(E) is the trap. More study hours among participants seems to undercut the program — but it does not change the conclusion either way as cleanly as (D), because tutoring sessions are a form of study, and the program could be exactly what induced the extra studying; extra hours could be the mechanism through which the program works rather than a rival cause. (C) Curving could complicate interpreting absolute grades, but with the same curve applied to both groups the comparison still reflects relative performance. (B) Tutor capacity bears on feasibility of the mandate, not on whether tutoring causes improvement. (A) Satisfaction elsewhere is irrelevant to this causal claim. Only (D) decisively moves the conclusion.

promptHTML:
After a regional grocery chain replaced its standard checkout lanes with self-service kiosks, the average time a customer spent waiting in line fell by nearly 40%. Yet over the same period, the proportion of shoppers who reported being dissatisfied with the speed of checkout actually rose sharply.

Which of the following, if true, best explains the apparent discrepancy between the shorter wait times and the increased dissatisfaction with checkout speed?
options: Scanning and bagging items oneself at a kiosk takes most customers noticeably longer than it took a trained cashier to do the same work.
The chain installed fewer total checkout points than before, so that during peak hours all kiosks were frequently occupied at once.
Customers who use self-service kiosks tend to purchase fewer items per visit than those who used the old standard lanes.
A competing grocery chain in the same region kept its staffed checkout lanes and advertised them heavily.
The kiosks were programmed to display promotional offers on screen while customers waited for an attendant to clear errors.
explanation: The paradox: waiting in line dropped 40%, yet dissatisfaction with checkout speed rose. Resolution must reconcile less line-waiting with a worse perception of overall speed. (A) does exactly this: "checkout speed" as the customer experiences it includes the time spent at the register, not just the time waiting to reach it. If self-scanning is slower than a cashier, the total time from joining the line to finishing can rise even though the queue itself is shorter — so customers feel checkout got slower. (B) is the strongest trap: fewer checkout points would tend to lengthen wait times, contradicting the stated 40% drop, so it deepens rather than resolves the paradox. (C) fewer items would make checkout faster, deepening the paradox. (D) and (E) are irrelevant to why these shoppers, with shorter lines, feel speed worsened.

promptHTML:
A pharmaceutical firm ran a year-long trial of a new cholesterol drug. Among trial participants, those taking the drug had a 30% lower rate of heart attacks than those taking a placebo. When the same drug was later approved and prescribed to the general population, however, patients taking it showed no measurable reduction in heart-attack rates compared with similar untreated patients.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the discrepancy between the trial result and the general-population result?
options: Patients in the general population who were prescribed the drug had, on average, higher baseline cholesterol than the trial participants.
The placebo group in the trial was larger than the group that received the active drug.
Heart attacks have many causes besides high cholesterol, several of which the drug does not address.
The drug also produces a modest reduction in blood pressure as a side effect.
The drug must be taken daily without interruption to lower cholesterol, and trial participants — unlike most prescribed patients — were monitored to ensure they never missed a dose.
explanation: The discrepancy is between a strong trial effect and a null real-world effect for the same drug. The resolver must identify a difference between trial conditions and ordinary prescribing. (E) supplies it: efficacy depends on perfect adherence, which the trial enforced through monitoring but the general population does not achieve — so in practice the drug's effect washes out. (C) is the classic trap: it's true and tempting, but it applies equally to the trial and the general population, so it cannot explain why the drug worked in one setting and not the other. (B) group size differences don't bias the rate comparison and don't differ between settings. (D) a blood-pressure benefit would, if anything, make the drug look more effective in the population, deepening the paradox. (A) higher baseline cholesterol would, if anything, leave more room for benefit, not explain a null result.

promptHTML:
City planners widened a heavily congested commuter highway from four lanes to six, expecting average rush-hour travel times along the corridor to fall. For the first month after the wider road opened, travel times did drop. But within a year, average rush-hour travel times along the same corridor had returned to exactly what they were before the widening.

Which of the following, if true, does most to explain why the travel-time improvement disappeared?
options: The construction work required to widen the highway took longer to complete than the planners had originally estimated.
Faster initial travel times led many commuters who had previously used side streets or commuted at off-peak hours to begin driving the highway during rush hour.
Some commuters switched from driving to a newly expanded commuter rail line that runs parallel to the highway.
The cost of widening the highway exceeded the budget the city had allocated for the project.
The widened highway required more frequent resurfacing than the original four-lane road had.
explanation: Paradox: extra capacity gave a temporary improvement that fully evaporated. The resolution is the well-known "induced demand" mechanism. (B) names it: the initial speed gain attracted new rush-hour drivers (from side streets and off-peak times) until congestion rebuilt to the old equilibrium — precisely why times returned to baseline. (C) is the key trap: commuters leaving the highway for rail would reduce highway traffic and help preserve the improvement, so it deepens the paradox. (A) construction delay doesn't bear on why times rose after the road opened and initially improved. (D) cost overrun is irrelevant to travel time. (E) resurfacing frequency, by itself, doesn't explain a steady return to the exact prior travel time during normal operation.

promptHTML:
A software company introduced a generous referral bonus: any employee who referred a candidate who was hired received a large cash payment. In the year after the program launched, the number of candidates referred by employees roughly tripled. Yet the number of new hires who came through employee referrals was slightly lower than it had been the year before the bonus existed.

Which of the following, if true, best explains the surprising drop in referral hires despite the surge in referrals?
options: The cash bonus was paid only after a referred hire completed six months of employment with the company.
The company's total number of new hires from all sources increased substantially during the year the bonus was offered.
Several competing firms launched similar referral-bonus programs during the same year.
Employees who referred candidates were, on average, more experienced than employees who did not.

Before the bonus existed, employees referred only candidates they personally judged to be strong fits, whereas the bonus led them to refer many acquaintances regardless of suitability, lowering the share of referrals the company chose to hire.
explanation: Three times as many referrals but fewer referral hires means the hire rate per referral collapsed. (E) explains the mechanism directly: the bonus changed referrer behavior from selective (strong fits) to indiscriminate, so even though referrals tripled, the fraction actually hired fell far enough that absolute hires dipped. That reconciles a surge in volume with a drop in output. (B) is the trap: more total hires from all sources would, if anything, predict more referral hires too, so it deepens the paradox. (A) a delayed payout affects when bonuses are paid, not how many referrals convert to hires. (D) the experience of referrers doesn't bear on hire conversion of the referrals. (C) competitors' programs might affect the candidate pool generally but don't explain why this company's tripled referrals yielded fewer hires.

promptHTML:
A national park introduced an online reservation system requiring all visitors to book an entry time slot in advance, intending to reduce overcrowding at the most popular trailheads. In the first season under the new system, the total number of visitors to the park fell by about 15%. Even so, park rangers reported that the most popular trailheads were more crowded at peak times than they had been before reservations were required.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the popular trailheads became more crowded even as overall visitation fell?
options: The park raised its entrance fee at the same time it introduced the reservation system.
The reservation system allowed visitors to choose any available entry time slot, and the great majority chose the mid-morning slots, concentrating arrivals at the popular trailheads into a few hours.
Visitors with reservations spent on average more total time inside the park than visitors had before.
The reservation website occasionally crashed during the first weeks of the season, frustrating some prospective visitors.
Many casual visitors who previously wandered to quieter trailheads were deterred by the reservation requirement and stopped visiting the park entirely.
explanation: Fewer visitors overall, yet worse peak crowding at the popular trailheads, means the timing or distribution of visits shifted. (B) resolves it: by letting everyone self-select slots, the system funneled most arrivals into the same mid-morning window at the same popular spots, so peak-time density rose even as the daily total fell. (E) is the strongest distractor — it explains the 15% drop in total visitation, but if those lost visitors used quieter trailheads, their departure would relieve pressure elsewhere, not increase crowding at the popular ones; it deepens rather than resolves the paradox. (A) higher fees would tend to reduce crowding everywhere. (C) longer stays could add some crowding but doesn't explain concentration at peak times at the popular sites specifically. (D) website crashes reduce visitors, deepening the paradox.

promptHTML:
An airline replaced the older planes on its busiest route with newer aircraft that burn 20% less fuel per mile flown. Fuel is the airline's single largest operating cost on that route. Over the following year, however, the airline's total fuel costs on that route increased compared with the year before, even though fuel prices per gallon were unchanged.

Which of the following, if true, best resolves the apparent contradiction?
options: Because the newer aircraft are quieter and more comfortable, the airline was able to add many additional flights on the route and fill them, so total miles flown rose by more than 20%.
The newer aircraft require a different grade of jet fuel than the older planes did.
Maintenance costs for the newer aircraft were lower than for the older planes.
The newer aircraft were more expensive to purchase and finance than the older planes they replaced.
A competing airline reduced its fares on the same route during the year.
explanation: Fuel per mile dropped 20% and the per-gallon price was flat, yet total fuel cost rose. Total fuel cost = (fuel per mile) × (miles flown) × (price per gallon). With the first and third factors not increasing, only a rise in miles flown can push the total up. (A) supplies exactly that: the airline expanded flights enough that total miles rose by more than 20%, overwhelming the per-mile efficiency gain. (D) and (C) concern purchase, financing, or maintenance costs — not fuel costs, so they're outside the scope of the contradiction. (B) the grade of fuel doesn't change cost if the per-gallon price is stated as unchanged. (E) a competitor's fares affect demand and revenue but, without telling us flights or miles increased, do not explain higher fuel consumption.

promptHTML:
A hospital introduced a new triage protocol that, according to several controlled studies, correctly identifies high-risk emergency patients more accurately than the protocol it replaced. In the two years since adopting it, the hospital has documented that the death rate among patients its triage system classifies as "high-risk" has risen, while the death rate among those classified as "low-risk" has fallen.

Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain these changes in death rates without implying that the new protocol performs worse than the old one?
options: The total number of patients arriving at the hospital's emergency department increased over the two-year period.

By more accurately identifying genuinely high-risk patients, the new protocol moved many borderline patients — who were previously labeled high-risk but usually survived — into the low-risk category, leaving the high-risk group composed of sicker patients on average.
Some patients classified as low-risk under the new protocol chose to seek care at other hospitals.
The new protocol takes slightly longer for staff to administer than the old protocol did.
The hospital hired additional emergency physicians during the same two-year period.
explanation: This is a classification-mix (stage-migration) paradox: each group's death rate can change purely because who is in each group changed, even if treatment quality is constant or improved. (B) gives the mechanism: a more accurate protocol strips relatively healthy borderline patients out of the high-risk bucket (raising that bucket's average severity, hence its death rate) and adds those likely-survivors to the low-risk bucket (lowering its death rate). Both shifts follow from better classification — satisfying the requirement that the protocol not be worse. (D) longer administration time doesn't explain divergent rate changes between groups. (A) more patients overall doesn't change the composition logic. (E) more physicians would tend to lower death rates in both groups, not raise one. (C) low-risk patients leaving wouldn't raise the high-risk death rate and isn't tied to severity.

promptHTML:
Critics of the new municipal bike-share program argue that it will fail because the city's three earlier attempts at car-sharing all collapsed within two years. This reasoning treats the fate of the car-sharing ventures as a reliable guide to what will happen to bike-sharing. But car-sharing and bike-sharing differ in cost, regulatory burden, and the demographics of likely users; the earlier failures therefore tell us little about the prospects of the current program. The bike-share program may well succeed despite its predecessors' record.

In the argument above, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first identifies the pattern of reasoning the author endorses; the second states the conclusion that follows from that pattern.
The first is an objection the author rejects; the second restates the position of the critics in different terms.
The first is the main conclusion of the argument; the second is evidence offered in support of that conclusion.
The first is a premise the author accepts; the second is a competing prediction the author dismisses.
The first characterizes the reasoning the author goes on to challenge; the second is the author's own conclusion.
explanation:
Map the structure. The critics' argument is described in the first sentence. The first boldface ("This reasoning treats the fate of the car-sharing ventures as a reliable guide...") characterizes the critics' inference — and the very next word, "But," signals that the author is about to attack it. So the first boldface is the reasoning the author challenges, not endorses. The author then gives a disanalogy (different cost, regulation, users) and closes with the second boldface ("may well succeed"), which is the author's own conclusion. That is exactly choice E.

Why the traps fail: (A) says the author endorses the first portion's pattern — but the "But" shows the author rejects it, so A inverts the author's stance. (B) calls the second boldface a restatement of the critics' position; in fact it is the opposite of the critics' position (they predict failure, the author predicts possible success). (C) mislabels the first boldface as the main conclusion, but it is a description of someone else's reasoning, and the author's conclusion is the second boldface, not the first. (D) wrongly says the author accepts the first portion as a premise, when the author's whole point is to undermine it. The answer is E.

promptHTML:
A pharmaceutical firm's analysts recommend raising the price of its only patented drug, reasoning that because demand for the drug has been insensitive to past price increases, a further increase will boost revenue. It is true that previous increases did not measurably reduce the number of units sold. However, those increases all occurred before any therapeutic substitute existed; a rival's substitute is now expected to reach the market within the year. Once that substitute is available, even a modest price increase could drive a substantial share of patients to switch.

In the argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first is an assumption on which the analysts' recommendation depends; the second identifies a flaw in that assumption.
The first is evidence the author rejects as inaccurate; the second is the author's reason for rejecting it.
The first is the recommendation the author opposes; the second is the reason the analysts give for it.
The first is a finding that the analysts cite in support of their recommendation and that the author concedes; the second is the consideration the author uses to undercut that recommendation.
The first states the author's main conclusion; the second provides evidence for that conclusion.
explanation:
Trace the moves. The analysts recommend a price increase, citing past insensitivity of demand. The first boldface ("previous increases did not measurably reduce the number of units sold") is that very factual finding — and the author signals agreement with "It is true that...," i.e., the author concedes it. Then "However" introduces a changed condition (a substitute is coming), and the second boldface states the upshot the author uses to undercut the recommendation. That is precisely choice D: a conceded supporting finding, then the consideration that weighs against the recommendation.

Why the traps fail: (C) calls the first boldface the recommendation; the recommendation is to raise the price, which is stated in the first sentence, not the boldface — the first boldface is a piece of evidence the analysts rely on. (E) says the first boldface is the author's main conclusion, but the author's position is critical of the price increase, and that critical point lives in the second boldface, not the first. (A) mislabels the first boldface as an "assumption"; it is an observed fact the author grants, not an unstated assumption. (B) is the most tempting trap: it claims the author rejects the first boldface as inaccurate — but "It is true that" shows the author accepts it; what the author disputes is the inference drawn from it, not its accuracy. The answer is D.

promptHTML:
Economist: Some commentators claim that the recent surge in start-up formation proves the new tax credit for entrepreneurs is working. The surge did indeed begin in the same quarter the credit took effect. Yet that same quarter also saw a sharp, unrelated drop in corporate hiring, which pushed many laid-off workers to start their own ventures out of necessity. The tax credit, then, need not be the cause of the increase in start-ups, even granting that the two coincided in time.

In the economist's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first is evidence the economist offers for the main conclusion; the second is that main conclusion.
The first is a claim the economist disputes; the second is an alternative explanation that, if true, would establish the commentators' position.
The first is the conclusion the commentators draw; the second is the economist's main conclusion, which contradicts it.
The first is a fact the economist accepts and that the commentators take as decisive; the second is the economist's conclusion that this fact is not decisive.
The first is the economist's main conclusion; the second is a concession the economist makes to the opposing view.
explanation:
Identify the parties. The commentators conclude that the credit is working, treating the timing coincidence as proof. The first boldface ("The surge did indeed begin in the same quarter the credit took effect") is that coincidence stated as a fact — "did indeed" shows the economist accepts it, and it is the very thing the commentators treat as decisive. The economist then supplies a rival cause (necessity-driven start-ups from layoffs) and reaches the second boldface: the credit need not be the cause. That is the economist's conclusion that the conceded fact is not decisive — choice D.

Why the traps fail: (C) says the first boldface is the commentators' conclusion; it is not — the commentators' conclusion is that the credit is working, whereas the boldface is just the timing fact both sides accept. (A) calls the first boldface the economist's own supporting evidence for his conclusion; but the timing fact actually supports the commentators' view — the economist's real evidence is the layoff explanation, which is not boldfaced. (B) wrongly says the second boldface, if true, would establish the commentators' position; it does the reverse — it weakens their causal claim. (E) inverts roles by calling the first boldface the main conclusion; the main conclusion is the second boldface. The answer is D.

promptHTML:
Spokesperson: Our competitor asserts that its delivery network is faster than ours because it operates more regional warehouses. Greater warehouse count does tend to shorten the average distance a package must travel. But our routing software re-optimizes every shipment in real time, which more than offsets the distance disadvantage, so our average delivery time is in fact the lower of the two. Warehouse count alone, therefore, does not determine which network is faster.

In the spokesperson's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first is the spokesperson's primary evidence; the second is the competitor's response to that evidence.
The first is the spokesperson's main conclusion; the second is a restatement of it.
The first acknowledges a general tendency that favors the competitor's claim; the second is the conclusion the spokesperson draws against that claim.
The first is the competitor's conclusion; the second is the spokesperson's evidence against it.
The first is an assumption the spokesperson rejects; the second explains why it should be rejected.
explanation:
Lay out the structure. The competitor argues: more warehouses ⇒ faster. The first boldface ("Greater warehouse count does tend to shorten the average distance") concedes a general tendency that supports the competitor — "does tend to" marks acknowledgment, not endorsement of the full claim. The spokesperson then introduces a counter-factor (real-time routing) and concludes in the second boldface that warehouse count alone does not settle which network is faster. That matches choice C: a concession favoring the opponent, then the author's contrary conclusion.

Why the traps fail: (D) labels the first boldface the competitor's conclusion, but the competitor's conclusion is "our network is faster"; the boldface is only a general tendency the spokesperson grants. (B) says the first boldface is the main conclusion and the second merely restates it — but the two say different things (one concedes a tendency, the other denies that tendency is decisive), and only the second is the author's conclusion. (E) calls the first boldface an assumption the spokesperson rejects; the spokesperson accepts it as true, disputing only its decisiveness. (A) treats the second boldface as the competitor's reply, but it is plainly the spokesperson's own closing conclusion ("therefore"). The answer is C.

promptHTML:
Biologist: A widely held view holds that the songbird population in the valley is shrinking because of the spread of a nonnative predator. The predator's range has indeed expanded across the valley over the past decade. But over that same decade, a fungal blight destroyed most of the berry shrubs the songbirds feed on, and population declines have been steepest precisely where the blight, not the predator, hit hardest. The loss of the food source is a better explanation of the decline than the spread of the predator is.

In the biologist's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first is the biologist's main conclusion; the second is a concession to the prevailing view.
The first is the evidence the biologist relies on most heavily; the second is the conclusion that evidence supports.
The first is a fact consistent with the prevailing view that the biologist does not contest; the second is the rival explanation the biologist concludes is superior.
The first is the prevailing view's conclusion; the second is the biologist's evidence against it.
The first is a finding the biologist shows to be false; the second is the conclusion that follows once it is discarded.
explanation:
Sort the claims. The prevailing view: predator spread is causing the decline. The first boldface ("The predator's range has indeed expanded") is a fact that fits that view — "indeed" signals the biologist does not contest it. The biologist then presents a competing cause (the blight wiping out the food source, with declines worst where the blight was worst) and concludes in the second boldface that the food-loss explanation is superior. That is choice C.

Why the traps fail: (D) calls the first boldface the prevailing view's conclusion; the conclusion is "the predator is shrinking the population," whereas the boldface is only the range-expansion fact, which both sides accept. (A) inverts the roles, naming the first boldface the main conclusion; the biologist's conclusion is the second boldface. (B) says the first boldface is the evidence the biologist relies on most; in fact the biologist's load-bearing evidence is the blight correlation, and the first boldface supports the opposing view. (E) is the strongest trap: it claims the biologist shows the first boldface to be false — but "indeed" concedes its truth; the biologist disputes only whether it is the best explanation, not whether the range actually expanded. The answer is C.

promptHTML:
Policy analyst: A proposal would cut the city bus fare in half to relieve highway congestion. If lower fares drew a large number of current drivers onto buses, highway traffic would ease noticeably. However, surveys consistently show that the people most likely to switch to buses in response to a fare cut are not drivers but current pedestrians and cyclists, who add nothing to highway traffic in the first place. The fare cut, then, is unlikely to relieve highway congestion to any meaningful degree.

In the policy analyst's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first states a condition under which the proposal would achieve its aim; the second is the analyst's conclusion that the condition is unlikely to be met in the relevant way.
The first is an objection to the proposal; the second is the analyst's reply defending the proposal.
The first is the analyst's main conclusion; the second is the evidence supporting it.
The first is a prediction the analyst endorses; the second is a competing prediction the analyst rejects.
The first is the proposal's stated goal; the second is the means proposed to achieve that goal.
explanation:
Read the logic. The proposal aims to relieve congestion via a fare cut. The first boldface is conditional: "If lower fares drew a large number of current drivers onto buses, highway traffic would ease." It states the condition under which the proposal would work — the analyst does not assert the condition holds, only what would follow if it did. The survey evidence then shows the switchers are pedestrians and cyclists, not drivers, so the condition is not met in the way that matters; the second boldface concludes the cut is unlikely to relieve congestion. That is choice A.

Why the traps fail: (C) names the first boldface the main conclusion, but it is a hypothetical, and the actual conclusion is the second boldface. (E) misreads the first boldface as the goal and the second as the means; the goal (relieve congestion) and means (cut fares) are both in the first sentence, not the boldface. (D) calls the first boldface a prediction the analyst endorses; but it is conditional — the analyst neither asserts the antecedent nor predicts the consequent will occur, and in fact argues the trigger fails. (B) reverses the analyst's stance: the second boldface attacks the proposal, it does not defend it. The answer is A.

promptHTML:
Manager: We should adopt the four-day workweek because the pilot team that tried it reported higher job satisfaction. Higher satisfaction on that team is exactly what we would expect if the shorter week were genuinely beneficial. But the pilot team was made up entirely of volunteers who had lobbied for the change, so their enthusiasm may reflect getting what they asked for rather than any real advantage of the schedule itself. The pilot's satisfaction results, therefore, are weak grounds for rolling the policy out company-wide.

In the manager's argument, the two portions in boldface play which of the following roles?
options: The first is evidence the author uses to support adopting the policy; the second is the author's endorsement of the policy.
The first describes what the cited result would indicate if a certain interpretation held; the second is the conclusion the author reaches after casting doubt on that interpretation.
The first is the position the author ultimately defends; the second is an objection the author overcomes.
The first is the conclusion of the argument; the second is a premise supporting it.
The first is an assumption the author shows to be true; the second is the consequence of that assumption.
explanation:
Follow the reasoning. Someone proposes the four-day week, citing the pilot team's higher satisfaction. The first boldface ("Higher satisfaction... is exactly what we would expect if the shorter week were genuinely beneficial") lays out what the result would indicate under the rosy interpretation — it does not assert that interpretation is correct. The author then undermines it: the team self-selected (volunteers who lobbied), so their enthusiasm may be confounded. The second boldface concludes the results are weak grounds for a company-wide rollout. That is choice B.

Why the traps fail: (D) and (C) both call the first boldface the conclusion or the author's defended position, but the author's actual conclusion is the second boldface, which is skeptical of the policy. (A) says the author uses the first boldface to support adopting the policy and that the second is an endorsement; in fact the author casts doubt on the result and the second boldface argues against a full rollout, the opposite of endorsement. (E) claims the author shows the first boldface (the favorable interpretation) to be true; the author does the reverse — the self-selection point is meant to call that interpretation into question. The answer is B.

promptHTML:
A consumer-electronics firm found that customers who downloaded its companion mobile app spent, on average, 40% more per year than customers who did not. The marketing director concluded that prompting more existing customers to install the app will raise the firm's average revenue per customer by a comparable amount.

The marketing director's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: treats a difference that holds on average as though it must hold for every individual customer
assumes that a trait distinguishing app users from non-users may itself be what drives both app adoption and higher spending
relies on a sample of customers too small to support any general conclusion about spending
draws a conclusion about future revenue from evidence that concerns only past revenue
takes the absence of evidence that the app reduces spending as evidence that it raises spending
explanation: The director observes a correlation (app users spend more) and infers that inducing app installation will cause higher spending. The flaw is a classic confound: the customers who already chose to install the app may be the firm's most engaged or highest-spending customers to begin with, so the same self-selecting trait could drive both behaviors. Pushing the app onto a different, less-engaged population need not transfer the spending gap. Option (B) names exactly this confound. (A) describes a division/average-to-individual error the argument never makes — the director reasons about averages throughout. (C) invents a sample-size problem the stimulus gives no basis for. (D) mislabels a routine past-to-future projection as a flaw; the real defect is causal, not temporal. (E) describes an appeal to ignorance, but the argument cites positive correlational evidence, not a lack of contrary evidence.

promptHTML:
Critic: The city's new bus-rapid-transit line was promoted as a way to cut downtown traffic. Yet in the year after it opened, the number of cars entering downtown each weekday actually rose by 3%. Clearly the line has failed to reduce traffic.

The critic's argument is most vulnerable to the objection that it
options: confuses the line's stated purpose with the actual intentions of the officials who built it
fails to consider that downtown car traffic might have risen even more had the line not been built
generalizes from a single year to a permanent trend in traffic levels
assumes without warrant that what is true of weekday traffic is also true of weekend traffic
presumes that because two events occurred in sequence, the first must have caused the second
explanation: The critic infers failure from the fact that traffic rose. But 'reduce traffic' is properly judged against the counterfactual: if an independent factor (population or job growth, a parallel highway closure) was pushing traffic up, the line could have lowered it relative to what it would otherwise have been, even as the raw count rose. Option (B) names this missing-counterfactual flaw precisely. (D) raises weekday-vs-weekend scope, but the claim at issue is downtown traffic generally, and the stimulus already specifies weekday data without overgeneralizing to weekends. (A) alleges an intentions-vs-stated-purpose equivocation the argument never trades on. (C) charges hasty generalization over time, but the conclusion is about whether the line reduced traffic, not about a permanent trend. (E) names post hoc reasoning, but the critic is denying an effect, not asserting a spurious cause.

promptHTML:
Manager: Our quality-control team flags a higher percentage of defective units on the products it inspects most thoroughly than on the products it inspects only briefly. Therefore, thorough inspection is making our products worse, and we should cut back on it to improve overall quality.

The manager's reasoning is flawed because it
options: treats a policy that benefits one product line as necessarily benefiting all product lines
overlooks the possibility that thorough inspection reveals defects that brief inspection simply misses
concludes that because thorough inspection is costly, it must also be ineffective
assumes that defective units are distributed evenly across all product lines
relies on the testimony of the quality-control team without verifying its accuracy
explanation: The higher defect rate under thorough inspection almost certainly reflects detection, not causation: thorough inspection finds defects that already exist, while brief inspection lets them through undetected. The manager mistakes a measurement artifact for a causal effect of inspecting. Option (B) names this directly — the correlation runs the opposite way from what is claimed. (D) raises an even-distribution assumption the argument never depends on. (E) attacks the team's reliability, but the flaw is in the manager's inference, not the data's accuracy. (A) describes a part-to-whole composition error not present here. (C) introduces cost, which the stimulus never mentions, and misstates the actual gap in reasoning.

promptHTML:
Economist: A truly free market always allocates resources efficiently. Skeptics point to the recent collapse in the regional housing market as a counterexample, claiming it shows free markets can misallocate resources badly. But that market was distorted by zoning rules and subsidies, so it was not a truly free market. Hence the collapse does nothing to undermine my claim.

The economist's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: defines 'free market' so that no possible market failure could ever count as evidence against the claim
relies on the authority of economists rather than on the housing data itself
bases a sweeping economic generalization on a single regional housing market
assumes that what is efficient for a region must be efficient for the whole economy
mistakes the absence of zoning rules for the presence of genuine market freedom
explanation: The economist protects the claim 'free markets always allocate efficiently' by ruling out, as 'not truly free,' any market that allocates inefficiently. This makes the claim immune to all counterevidence: any failure is redefined away. That is circular / no-true-Scotsman reasoning, captured by option (A). (C) reverses the direction of the argument — the economist is dismissing a single case, not generalizing from one. (E) gets the logic backward; the economist treats the presence of zoning as disqualifying, not the absence as qualifying. (D) raises a part-to-whole efficiency leap the argument does not make. (B) alleges an appeal to authority, but the economist appeals to a definition, not to expert standing.

promptHTML:
Public-health official: A new study reports that adults who take daily vitamin D supplements have notably lower rates of seasonal depression than adults who do not. To reduce seasonal depression nationwide, the government should therefore fund free vitamin D supplements for all adults.

The official's recommendation depends on which questionable assumption?
options: Vitamin D supplements are more cost-effective than other treatments for seasonal depression.
Seasonal depression is the most common form of depression among adults.
No adult who takes vitamin D supplements ever experiences seasonal depression.
Adults who currently take vitamin D would continue to do so if the supplements were free.
The lower depression rates among supplement-takers are due to the supplements rather than to other habits those adults share.

For much of the twentieth century, the textbook account of how wages are set treated the labor market as effectively competitive: many employers bid for workers who could costlessly move between jobs, so any firm that tried to pay below the prevailing wage would lose its entire workforce, and each worker was paid a wage equal to the value of what an additional hour of their labor produced. Within this framework, a legally imposed minimum wage above the competitive level could only reduce employment, because firms confronted with a wage floor would hire fewer workers than the market would otherwise sustain.

An older but long-marginalized alternative, the theory of monopsony, complicates this picture. A monopsonistic employer faces an upward-sloping supply of labor: to attract more workers it must raise the wage it offers, and—absent the ability to pay each worker a different rate—it must raise the wage paid to existing workers as well. The marginal cost of an additional hire therefore exceeds that worker’s wage. A profit-maximizing monopsonist responds by hiring fewer workers and paying a lower wage than a competitive market would. Crucially, within a band, a minimum wage can compel such an employer to pay more and employ more, because it severs the link between the wage and the marginal cost of hiring.

Recent empirical work has revived interest in this once-peripheral model. Studies exploiting regional variation in minimum-wage increases have frequently found employment effects far smaller than the competitive model predicts, and sometimes none at all. Proponents read these results as evidence that frictions—search costs, geographic immobility, imperfect information—confer monopsony power on many ordinary employers, not merely the isolated company town of textbook caricature. Skeptics counter that null employment effects are also consistent with firms absorbing higher labor costs through reduced profits, higher prices, or slower future hiring that conventional studies fail to detect. What seems increasingly difficult to defend, however, is the once-reflexive assumption that the competitive model is the natural default and monopsony the exotic exception.
The passage is primarily concerned with

demonstrating that minimum-wage laws reliably raise both wages and employment in most labor markets
tracing the historical reasons that the theory of monopsony was marginalized for most of the twentieth century
adjudicating a dispute between proponents and skeptics by showing that the skeptics’ objections cannot withstand scrutiny
arguing that search costs and geographic immobility are the principal determinants of wages in modern economies

That arc—a revived model plus evidence unsettling the default view—is exactly choice A.

Atmospheric nitrogen is abundant—it constitutes roughly 78% of the air—yet most organisms cannot use it, because the triple bond joining the two nitrogen atoms in N₂ is among the most stable in chemistry. Only certain prokaryotes, the diazotrophs, possess nitrogenase, the enzyme that cleaves this bond and reduces N₂ to ammonia. Among the most studied diazotrophs are rhizobia, soil bacteria that infect the roots of legumes and inhabit specialized swellings called nodules. There the bacterium trades fixed nitrogen for carbon compounds supplied by the plant, a reciprocity long offered as a textbook emblem of mutualism.

Yet the relationship is less placid than that emblem suggests. Nitrogenase is irreversibly poisoned by oxygen, while the bacterium's own respiration—needed to power the energy-hungry reaction—demands oxygen. The legume resolves this contradiction by synthesizing leghemoglobin, a pigment that binds oxygen tightly enough to keep the enzyme's surroundings nearly anoxic, yet releases it fast enough to sustain respiration. The plant, in other words, does not merely host the bacterium; it actively engineers a chemical environment without which fixation would be impossible.

This dependence has tempted some agronomists to imagine transferring nitrogen-fixing capacity to cereals such as wheat and rice, which would lessen reliance on the synthetic fertilizers whose manufacture consumes vast quantities of fossil fuel. The difficulty is that the legume's contribution is not a single transferable gene but an integrated physiology—nodule formation, oxygen regulation, and a carbon subsidy so large that fixation can cost the plant a fifth of its photosynthetic output. A cereal endowed with nitrogenase but lacking these supports might fix little nitrogen while paying a steep metabolic toll. The symbiosis endures, this analysis suggests, not because it is effortless but because each partner has evolved to absorb costs the other cannot.
Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The rhizobia–legume symbiosis, far from being an effortless exchange, depends on a costly and integrated set of plant adaptations that complicate efforts to transplant nitrogen fixation into other crops.
Because synthetic nitrogen fertilizers consume large amounts of fossil fuel, agronomists have concluded that engineering nitrogen fixation into cereals is the only sustainable path forward.
Leghemoglobin is the single most important factor in nitrogen fixation, since without it the bacterium's nitrogenase would be destroyed by the oxygen its own respiration requires.
The mutualism between rhizobia and legumes is best understood as a balanced exchange in which each partner contributes equally and neither bears a disproportionate cost.
Nitrogenase is the sole enzyme capable of breaking the nitrogen triple bond, and its sensitivity to oxygen makes biological nitrogen fixation impossible outside of root nodules.
explanation:
The passage moves from the textbook image of mutualism, to the hidden complexity (the oxygen paradox and leghemoglobin), to the practical upshot that the legume's contribution is an integrated, costly physiology rather than a transferable gene—which is why engineering fixation into cereals is hard. Choice A captures that arc.

B is too extreme and distorts the text: the author presents cereal engineering as a tempting but problematic aspiration, never as 'the only sustainable path.' E overstates: the passage says fixation in legumes occurs in nodules but never claims fixation is impossible outside nodules—other free-living diazotrophs exist (the broader category 'diazotrophs' is introduced). C fixes on one detail (leghemoglobin) and inflates it into the main point, ignoring the engineering theme. D contradicts the passage's closing claim that each partner absorbs costs the other cannot—the author explicitly undercuts the 'balanced/placid' picture.

Among the most studied diazotrophs are rhizobia, soil bacteria that infect the roots of legumes and inhabit specialized swellings called nodules. The legume resolves this contradiction by synthesizing leghemoglobin, a pigment that binds oxygen tightly enough to keep the enzyme's surroundings nearly anoxic, yet releases it fast enough to sustain respiration. For much of the twentieth century, the collapse of the Western Roman Empire was narrated as a story of decline and fall: a once-vigorous civilization, sapped by moral decay, fiscal exhaustion, and barbarian violence, simply ceased to function. This “catastrophist” reading, inherited from Gibbon and sharpened by mid-century scholars, treated the fifth century as a rupture — the lights of urban, literate, monetized life going dark across the West.

Drawing on continuities in law, language, and Christian institutions, these historians argued that Rome did not so much fall as gradually metamorphose into the early medieval world, with Germanic elites accommodating themselves to Roman administrative forms rather than demolishing them. More recently, a third group of scholars has pushed back against the transformationists, marshalling archaeological evidence — coin finds, pottery distributions, skeletal data, the shrinking of cattle — to argue that material living standards did, in fact, decline sharply and rapidly. Yet these archaeologically minded historians do not simply revive the old catastrophism; they reject its moralizing causes while accepting its claim of genuine rupture. The disappearance of mass-produced goods, they contend, is not a matter of interpretive emphasis but a measurable fact, and one that the transformationist emphasis on elite cultural continuity conveniently overlooks.

The dispute is therefore not merely about evidence but about which evidence counts. Where transformationists read texts produced by a surviving literate elite, the materialists read the silent residue of ordinary life. Economists have long modeled the diffusion of a new technology as an S-shaped curve: adoption begins slowly among a few pioneers, accelerates as the technology proves itself and information spreads, and finally plateaus once the pool of potential users is saturated. The standard “epidemic” account attributes this shape to the spread of information—potential adopters learn of the innovation by contact with those who have already adopted it, much as a contagion propagates through a population. On this view, the chief barrier to diffusion is ignorance, and the chief remedy is communication.

Yet the epidemic model struggles to explain why some technologies of demonstrable superiority diffuse over decades rather than months, long after knowledge of them has become universal. A competing “rank” account holds that firms differ in the benefit they would derive from adopting, so that diffusion reflects not the spread of awareness but the gradual arrival of conditions under which adoption becomes profitable for successively less-suited firms. A third, “stock” account emphasizes that the return to adopting often falls as more firms adopt—because, say, the cost advantage of a new process erodes once competitors share it—so that later adopters face weaker incentives than pioneers did.

These accounts are frequently presented as rivals, and empirical studies have sometimes pitted them against one another, asking which best fits a given diffusion path. That framing, however, mistakes the question. The mechanisms are not mutually exclusive; a single episode of diffusion may be governed by information spread early on, by heterogeneity in firm benefit throughout, and by erosion of returns near the end. The persistent search for a single dominant mechanism has, if anything, obscured the more useful task of specifying the conditions under which each becomes salient. Until diffusion research embraces that compositional view, its models will continue to fit curves while explaining little.

promptHTML:
For much of the twentieth century, the term decorative functioned in art criticism as a quiet insult. To call a painting decorative was to imply that it pleased the eye without engaging the mind — that it was, in the influential vocabulary of the formalist critics, mere ornament rather than serious art. This usage rested on an unexamined hierarchy: the “significant” work supposedly subordinated surface pattern to an underlying structure of meaning, whereas the decorative work let pattern reign unchecked. The hierarchy was rarely defended; it was simply assumed, and on its strength entire traditions — textile design, Islamic ornament, much of women's craft — were filed away as minor.

Recent scholarship has begun to dismantle this assumption, though not always in the way its proponents suppose. Some revisionists merely invert the old hierarchy, celebrating the decorative as a subversive force that resists the “masculine” demand for depth. This move, however, leaves the underlying opposition between surface and meaning intact; it simply switches which pole is praised. A more searching line of argument questions the opposition itself. On this view, the very distinction between a meaningful structure and a merely pleasing surface is a historical artifact, one that certain modernist critics needed in order to police the boundaries of high art. Where no such boundary is presupposed — in many non-Western traditions, for instance — pattern and significance are not rivals but aspects of a single achievement.

The second argument is the more powerful, but it carries a cost its advocates seldom acknowledge: if the surface–depth distinction is wholly dissolved, criticism loses a vocabulary it has long used to discriminate the ambitious work from the merely charming. The challenge, then, is not to abolish the distinction but to historicize it — to recognize when it illuminates and when it merely excludes.

options: The formalist critics of the twentieth century were wrong to treat textile design, Islamic ornament, and women's craft as minor traditions unworthy of serious study.
Recent revisionist scholarship has successfully overturned the formalist hierarchy by demonstrating that decorative art is a subversive force resisting the demand for depth.
The distinction between meaningful structure and pleasing surface is a historical artifact invented by modernist critics, and criticism would be better off discarding it entirely.
Non-Western artistic traditions are superior to Western ones because they refuse to treat pattern and significance as rivals.

Although the term "decorative" was long used pejoratively, the most defensible response is not to invert or abolish the surface–depth distinction but to recognize the historically contingent limits of its usefulness.
explanation:
The passage moves through three positions: the old pejorative usage, two revisionist replies (inversion and dissolution), and the author's own qualified verdict in the final paragraph — that the surface–depth distinction should be neither abolished nor merely inverted but historicized. Option E captures exactly this arc and the author's stance.

A is true but partial: the harm done to minor traditions is a supporting detail in paragraph 1, not the overall point, and A says nothing about the author's central recommendation. B overstates and misattributes: the author calls the inversion move shallow ("leaves the underlying opposition intact") and does not endorse it. C states the dissolution argument the author explicitly resists — the author warns that abolishing the distinction has "a cost" and concludes the distinction should be kept but historicized, the opposite of "discarding it entirely." D is a value claim the passage never makes; non-Western traditions are cited only as an example where the boundary is not presupposed, not as superior.

When economists first proposed pricing carbon emissions, the appeal was its elegant simplicity: attach a cost to each ton of carbon dioxide released, and self-interested firms would, in aggregate, abate emissions wherever abatement was cheapest. Two instruments emerged. A carbon tax fixes the price of emitting and lets the resulting quantity of emissions float; a cap-and-trade system fixes the quantity by issuing a limited number of tradable permits and lets the price float. For decades, advocates treated the choice between them as a matter of administrative taste, since under textbook assumptions of perfect information the two converge on identical outcomes.

That equivalence, however, dissolves once uncertainty is admitted. Martin Weitzman's seminal analysis showed that when the marginal cost of abatement is poorly known but the marginal benefit of an additional ton avoided is relatively flat — as it plausibly is for a pollutant whose damage accrues from a slowly accumulating global stock — a price instrument outperforms a quantity instrument, because it shields firms from the wild cost swings a fixed cap can impose. Where damages instead rise sharply past some threshold, a quantity cap is safer. Carbon, most economists now hold, belongs to the former case.

Yet the cleaner instrument has rarely prevailed politically. Cap-and-trade has spread further, partly because permits can be handed out free to incumbent emitters, converting a policy cost into a windfall that buys their acquiescence. When courts confront a statute whose words do not cleanly resolve the case before them, two interpretive traditions compete for primacy. Textualists insist that the enacted words, read in their ordinary public meaning at the time of passage, exhaust the legitimate sources of law; to reach behind the text for a legislature’s supposed intentions, they argue, is to substitute the judge’s preferences for the democratically ratified bargain. Purposivists counter that words are instruments of communication, and that a faithful reader must reconstruct the mischief a statute was meant to cure, consulting committee reports, prior law, and the broader scheme. Each side claims the mantle of restraint: textualists by binding judges to a fixed object, purposivists by binding them to the legislature’s actual project rather than its inartful phrasing.

Yet the dichotomy is overdrawn. No competent textualist reads a word in a vacuum; “ordinary meaning” is itself reconstructed from context, canons, and assumptions about a reasonable speaker’s aims—which is to say, from a thin theory of purpose. And no responsible purposivist treats a fragment of legislative history as a trump over clear enacted text, for the history was never voted on. The genuine disagreement is narrower: it concerns which contextual evidence is admissible and how much weight an unenacted source may bear.

That reframing suggests a constrained purposivism. Courts should begin with the text and resort to extrinsic purpose only when the words are genuinely ambiguous, and even then should privilege purpose evidence that the whole legislature plausibly shared over the stray remark of a single sponsor. Such a discipline neither fetishizes the dictionary nor licenses freewheeling reconstruction; it treats interpretation as the recovery of a public meaning that text and shared purpose jointly fix.
